newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan downbeat on Mideast summit, people angry.
newsitem.headline: Jordan downbeat on Mideast summit, people angry.

text.p: Jordan, facing growing popular anger against Israeli policies after it signed a 1994 peace treaty with the Jewish state, said on Thursday a Washington summit to rescue Middle East peace was "below expectations."

The summit ended on Wednesday without agreement on any of the substantial points the Arabs wanted settled, including closure of a tunnel Israel opened near Moslem holy shrines in Jerusalem last week that sparked bloody Arab-Israeli unrest.
"Certainly the summit was below expectations," Information Minister Marwan Muasher told reporters.

"Maybe it has averted a disaster in the short run by putting Palestinian-Israeli talks back on track but something has to be done as the present situation can't continue. We need to see implementation of accords signed between Israel and the PLO."
Israel and the Palestinians agreed in Washington only to end violence and keep talking about matters the Palestinians thought they agreed on with the former government a year ago.

Jordan, still legal custodian of Moslem holy shrines in Arab Jerusalem which it ruled together with the West Bank from 1952 until losing it to Israel in 1967, wanted peace talks to resume on all Arab-Israeli tracks to boost its controversial treaty.
The close ties Amman developed with Israel since the treaty are slowly souring because of Israel's tough peace policies.

Even officials, who sounded positive towards Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's hardline peace policies when he was elected in May and urged wary Arabs to give him a chance to show his intentions, now sound downbeat.

Jordan accused Israel this week of breaching articles of the treaty which recognised Jordan's "special role" over Moslem holy shrines in Arab Jerusalem, which Palestinians hope will be the capital of their future state -- an idea opposed by Israel.

"Half of the problem in which the king was interested...was Jerusalem and this was not solved," George Hawatmeh, chief editor of Jordan's only English-language daily, told Reuters. "But returning the Palestinian-Israeli talks to their track was more important at this stage."
Headlines on most state-controlled newspapers, using red ink letters, blamed Netanyahu and U.S. President Bill Clinton for the summit's failure.

Many of Jordan's 4.2 million population, a large part of which are of Palestinian origin, had their eyes glued to television on Wednesday night as Clinton announced the end of the summit, called to salvage Middle East peace after 73 Palestinians and Israelis were killed in the latest unrest.
But they saw the king and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat, both grim-faced, standing next to Clinton and Netanyahu and heard no good news to match their expectations.
Most Jordanians, reeling under severe economic hardship, growing unemployment and poverty, are already frustrated because the much-promised 1994 peace dividends have not materialised.
For the man in the street, the summit was a disaster.
It reinforced deep popular doubts about Israel's peace intentions and American willingness to pressure the Jewish state, its main ally in the region, to "achieve just peace".
The influential lslamic Action Front (IAF), the single largest political group in parliament, condemned the summit.
"Israel's intransigence can only be confronted with real Jihad (Moslem holy war)," said IAF deputy Bassam Ummoush.
Others predicted further violence in Palestinian areas.

Diplomats said the king would continue to face a difficult balancing act, maintaining relations with Arabs suspicious of his links to Israel while keeping a working relationship with Netanyahu to safeguard his treaty.
Because of close demographic, political and economic links, any development in Palestinian territories will affect Jordan.
"Any splash there will hit us here," one official said.
